opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one people sometimes misunderstand. Mathlib is an incredible achievement. It's a huge community effort, and it covers a lot of undergraduate and a good chunk of graduate-level mathematics. But it's obviously not all of mathematics. There are whole areas where the definitions just haven't been written down yet, or where the foundational lemmas you'd need to state a research-level result don't exist.

So the way I think about it is that a sufficiently capable system shouldn't treat Mathlib as a ceiling. It should treat it as a starting point. When a human mathematician works in a new area, they don't wait for someone else to have written the textbook. They build the definitions they need, prove the supporting lemmas, and develop the theory as they go. We want models that can do the same thing: auto-formalize the definitions, check that they actually capture the intended concept, build up the intermediate library, and then attack the main result.

Lean is really helpful here, because whatever the model builds is verified. If the model invents a bunch of new infrastructure, you don't have to trust it the way you'd have to trust an informal argument. The kernel checks it. The hard part, and I think this is where a lot of the interesting research is, is making sure the definitions mean what you think they mean. A proof can be perfectly correct and still be about the wrong object. So you need good ways for models, and humans working with models, to validate the statements and definitions, not just the proofs.

Over time I think this creates a flywheel. Models extend the formal library into new areas, which gives you more data and more scaffolding, which makes the models better at going further. Eventually I'd expect a lot of the growth of formalized mathematics to be driven by AI systems, with humans steering toward what's interesting and important. So Mathlib being incomplete isn't a fundamental blocker. It's more a description of where the frontier currently sits, and the goal is to push it outward.

r001.rationale: The response says Mathlib covers much but not all mathematics, with entire areas lacking definitions or foundational lemmas, and says models should extend the library beyond that frontier.

r002.rationale: It says models should build needed definitions, prove supporting lemmas, develop theory, and extend the formal library as they go.

r003.rationale: The response mentions auto-formalizing definitions, but does not describe translating informal descriptions of everyday situations into Lean code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is probably the single most common question we get, and it's a fair one. Mathlib is incredible, it's one of the great collaborative projects in mathematics, but it's still maybe a small fraction of what's actually in the literature. And if you train a model purely on what's already been formalized, the worry is that you've built something that can only prove theorems about objects that someone else already bothered to define.

The way I think about it is that there are really two separate problems hiding in there. One is the definitions problem: can the model work with mathematical objects that don't exist in the library yet? And the other is the proof problem: can it actually find proofs once the statement is pinned down?

On the definitions side, what we've found is that models are actually surprisingly good at autoformalization when you give them the right scaffolding. If you hand a model a paper that defines some new structure, it can propose a Lean definition, and then crucially, you can check that definition against the informal one by having the model prove some sanity-check lemmas. If the new definition doesn't let you prove the obvious properties that the paper claims, that's a signal that the formalization is wrong. So the formal system gives you a feedback loop that you simply don't have with natural language math. That's the thing that makes this tractable rather than hopeless.

On the proof side, I'd actually push back a little on the framing that Mathlib is the ceiling. The reason you want a big library is not that it contains the answer, it's that it contains the building blocks. Most of the proofs that matter in a new paper reuse a huge amount of standard machinery, compactness arguments, inequalities, basic algebraic manipulation. That stuff is in Mathlib. What's missing is usually a relatively thin layer of new definitions and a handful of new key lemmas on top. So the model's job is to build that layer, not rebuild analysis from scratch.

And then the thing that I think really changes the game is that the model's output can itself go back into the library. Every time a model formalizes a new definition and proves things about it, that becomes training data and it becomes infrastructure for the next problem. So you get this compounding effect where the frontier of what's formalized moves as a side effect of the model doing useful work. Humans doing this by hand is bottlenecked on how many people know Lean and have the patience for it. A model that's grinding on this around the clock doesn't have that bottleneck.

The honest caveat is that this gets much harder as you go up the abstraction ladder. Formalizing something in combinatorics or elementary number theory is pretty well understood. Formalizing modern algebraic geometry or large parts of analysis where the definitions themselves are subtle and there are multiple inequivalent ways to set things up, that's genuinely hard, and I don't think we've fully cracked it. But I think the direction is clear: the way you overcome the Mathlib limitation is you stop treating the library as fixed and start treating it as something the model is actively extending.

r001.rationale: It says Mathlib covers only a small fraction of the literature and describes its limits as a concern for models trained only on existing formalizations.

r002.rationale: It describes models proposing new Lean definitions and proving new lemmas, thereby extending the library beyond what has already been formalized.

r003.rationale: It discusses formalizing mathematical definitions from papers, not translating informal descriptions of everyday situations into Lean code.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that Mathlib isn’t a fixed boundary. If a model needs a result that isn’t in the library, it can state that result, prove it from more basic results, and then use it in the original proof. That’s what a human mathematician does: you discover that you need a lemma, you go prove the lemma, and you come back.

The hard part is figuring out which missing pieces are useful. You don’t want to formalize an entire textbook every time you encounter something new. You want the model to identify the right definitions and intermediate results, build those out, and have the proof checker verify them. Over time, that work can expand the library, so subsequent problems become easier. The library is a starting point for that process, rather than a ceiling.

r002.rationale: It describes adding missing results, definitions, and intermediate lemmas, but does not say models must create new mathematical theories beyond what humans have formalized.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss automatically translating informal descriptions of everyday situations into Lean code.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that Mathlib isn’t a fixed boundary. If a model needs a theorem that isn’t there, it can state that theorem, prove it, and then use it as a building block. And if the concepts it needs aren’t there, it can introduce definitions too.

The hard part is deciding what’s worth adding. You don’t just want a model generating thousands of lemmas that nobody will ever use. You want it to recognize a missing abstraction, develop enough theory around it, and make the original problem easier. That’s much closer to how mathematicians work.

So I’d expect a feedback loop: models initially rely heavily on the existing library, then gradually become capable of extending it. The proof checker still verifies each step, but the space of mathematics they can work in keeps growing.

r001.rationale: It says models may need theorems and concepts that Mathlib does not yet contain, identifying its current coverage as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It describes adding theorems, definitions, and enough theory around missing abstractions, but does not say models must create new mathematical theories beyond what humans have formalized.

r003.rationale: It discusses creating theorems and definitions in Mathlib, but says nothing about automatically translating informal descriptions of everyday situations into Lean code.
